cells.tense: You're in it now, mid-season, and your hands know the pace.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're tending right now, say what it needs from you this week and where that stops, then let it run at that size. A shape you can rest inside comes out of saying it plain.
cells.core:
You're in it now, and your hands know the pace. Care moves because the person or the work is mid-growth and you're not standing over it — you keep the conditions right and then let it alone. It doesn't drain you. You put the water down when the water's done.

A release that comes from finishing, not from quitting, is what's free to feed next. You'll know the moment something is complete, and you can let it go and mean it. Naming one thing you're tending, and saying what it needs this week and where that stops, puts a size on the care. A shape you can rest inside comes out of saying it plain.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's growing and you let it set its own pace.
cells.verb: tending what's growing without forcing it

cells.tense: You're living in a next moment that hasn't arrived, bracing for a need nobody has named yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding and write down, on one side of a page, what it's actually responsible for, and on the other what you'd do if the next thing doesn't come. Do it at the table you're at, in your own words. It leaves you an edge you can stand on.
cells.core:
A good week here looks ordinary: you carry something heavy without turning it into a campaign — you ask what's needed and you wait for a real answer. Lately the effort has gone ahead of the need. You're arranging for a future that can't be written yet, anticipating the next hard moment, doing for people what they haven't asked and might not want. From outside it looks like care. From inside it's a hold that won't loosen, and the person on the other end feels the grip.

The way back runs through standing in the middle of an open question without solving it early, which is harder than it sounds, because not-knowing reads as danger when you're braced. Picking one thing you're holding and setting down on paper what it's responsible for, and what you'd do if the next trouble doesn't arrive, leaves you an edge you can stand on.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing for what hasn't happened, and the grip is showing.
cells.verb: tending what's growing without forcing it

cells.tense: You're standing at a place you left, offering care that already has no one on the other end of it.
cells.ask: Do one small visible thing today for something already growing near you — water a plant, answer one message you've been holding, set out food — and stop there. It shows you there's a direction worth giving yourself to.
cells.core:
A good week here looks ordinary: you show up for people, you do the thing, and you don't disappear into it. Lately little of that happens. Nothing you start gets fed past the first week, and the standing-apart reads as having it handled. The independence isn't fake so much as it has nowhere to go — you're not around for what's growing, and not much is growing near you to be around for.

Pushing harder at the tired place doesn't help; it's the same block in different words. Do one small visible thing today for something already growing near you — water a plant, answer one message you've been holding, set out food — and stop there. It shows you there's a direction worth giving yourself to, and that the direction still works.
cells.sheetLine: You've stepped back from what was growing, and called it independence.
cells.verb: tending what's growing without forcing it

cells.tense: You're already holding a great deal, while the account you keep says none of it is yours to lay down.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to yourself or one person, that one thing you do for someone daily is yours to keep or lay down — and give a day's notice on the one that costs most. That sentence puts the caretaking back in your hands.
cells.core:
A good week here looks ordinary: the offering is chosen — you look after people because you decided to, and you know what it costs and where it stops. As things stand the role runs without you in the chair. People bring you their trouble, you carry it, and you'd say you're just keeping things going. The caring is real; the deciding is missing, and that's what empties you.

The step back is smaller than a change of life. Say once, out loud, that one thing you do for someone daily is yours to keep or lay down — then give a day's notice on the one that costs most. That's the line from which the rest can be decided.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying for people and calling it just life.
cells.verb: tending what's growing without forcing it
